This model asks two questions at once, about the same children: how many words does a child with Down syndrome understand at a given age, and what fraction of those words do they also say? The second question is what the joint structure exists for. Spoken vocabulary is modelled as understood vocabulary multiplied by a production ratio $q$, so _knowing more words_ and _saying more of the words you know_ are separated rather than confounded. Age here is a proxy for everything that happens over time ($A \rightarrow U$, $A \rightarrow S$, $U \rightarrow S$), not a cause in itself.

VG10 is the interpretive template the rest of the Down syndrome family follows, and was the headline Down syndrome joint model until 2026-08-19.

::: {.callout-important title="Superseded as the model of record on 2026-08-19"}
[VG20](../vg20/index.qmd) — this model plus one free correlation `rho_uq` between a child's comprehension and production-ratio random intercepts — replaced VG10 as the model of record for the Down syndrome joint understood + spoken estimands, after the four gates of [#224](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/224). VG10 is now a **development step** and supplies no reported number.

The **population-level** results below are not withdrawn: expected words on both outcomes and the production ratio are reproduced by VG20 inside VG10's own 89% interval at every reported age, which is what a correlation between two mean-zero deviations must do. What is superseded is everything **child-level**. VG10 draws each child's two deviations independently, which its own fitted deviations contradict — they correlate at +0.151 [0.106, 0.195] against a prior asserting zero, and VG20 puts the free parameter at +0.368 [0.287, 0.447]. The consequence is that VG10's subject-marginal intervals for words spoken are **too narrow**, by 9% at 90 months rising to 33% at 12, and every between-child DS-versus-TD spoken contrast derived from this model understated the Down syndrome side by about 15% on the logit scale.

Read this report for the lineage and for the trajectory results; read VG20's for anything about how much children differ from one another.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Which estimand each figure shows"}

Two different predictions run through this report, and confusing them is the easiest way to misread it.

- A **population-level** curve sets every random effect to zero. It is a conditional zero-effect trajectory — approximately the **median** child in the average study, not the average of children's curves, because the inverse-logit link is nonlinear — and its interval is uncertainty about that reference trajectory. In the summary tables these are the `p_population_*` and `Ey_population_*` columns.
- A **subject-marginal** prediction draws a new child's random effects as well. It answers _where would one more child fall?_, and it is much the wider of the two. In the summary tables these are the `p_subject_marginal_*` / `Ey_subject_marginal_*` columns, and the `Y_*` and `P(Y<=k)` columns, which are predictive counts for an unseen child.

Every figure below is labelled with which of the two it draws. In particular the **joint-trajectory figures are subject-marginal**: their bands are the range individual children occupy, not uncertainty in the average trajectory. The historical `p_*` and `Ey_*` columns keep their population-level meaning; the explicit `p_population_*` columns restate it so that no column's estimand has to be inferred.

:::

## Statistical model

Words understood are a bounded count out of the reference inventory, with a Beta-Binomial likelihood. On the logit scale the expected proportion understood is a straight-line developmental trend in age plus a Gaussian process term, which lets the curve bend away from the line by as much as the data support and no more.

Spoken words are modelled _through_ comprehension rather than beside it. For a row where both counts are present and logically nested, spoken words are drawn conditionally on the child's own observed understood count, $S \mid U \sim \operatorname{BetaBinomial}(U, q, \kappa_S)$, so the trials are the words that child actually understands. A row that carries no usable understood count — missing, out of range, or recording more spoken than understood words — falls back to the marginal form against the full reference inventory. A substantial minority of the spoken rows take that fallback, which matters when reading the spoken dispersion: it governs both branches.

The production ratio $q$ has the same shape as the understood trajectory — a straight line on the logit scale plus a Gaussian process term:

$$f_U(a, s, i) = \text{intercept}_U + \text{slope}_U \cdot a_z + \tilde g_U(a) + \delta_U[s] + \delta^{\text{subj}}_U[i]$$
$$h(a, s, i) = \text{intercept}_q + \text{slope}_q \cdot a_z + \tilde g_q(a) + \delta_q[s] + \delta^{\text{subj}}_q[i]$$

where $a_z$ is age standardised, $\delta[s]$ is the offset of study $s$, $\delta^{\text{subj}}[i]$ the offset of child $i$, and $\tilde g$ the anchored Gaussian process described below. The likelihood's $q$ is the _child's_ ratio, $\operatorname{logit}^{-1} h(a, s, i)$, including both random effects — not the population curve plotted later in this report.

Neither straight line is given a prior directly. Priors are placed instead on the expected proportion at two reference ages, which is a far more interpretable thing to have an opinion about than an intercept at age zero. One caution on reading them: the anchors parameterise the straight-line component only. The anchored Gaussian process below is pinned to zero at the reference age and orthogonalised against the trend on the observed rows, but it is not zero at the anchor ages themselves, so the fitted curve there is the anchor plus the process's contribution — the anchors are coordinates of the trend, not exact values of the fitted curve.

Children of the same age differ far more than a Binomial count would allow, so both likelihoods are Beta-Binomial with a dispersion that is itself allowed to change with age.

### Hierarchy

Study offsets are constrained to sum to zero, so the population curve is the _average study_ rather than an arbitrary reference study; an individual study offset therefore cannot be read as a free per-study level. Child offsets are ordinary random intercepts. All four random-effect blocks use the non-centred form $\delta = \tau z$, which is why the trace and pair plots show the raw $z$ variables and the scales $\tau$ separately.

### The GP anchor {#sec-gp-anchor}

This is the one structural change relative to VG09, and VG10's reason to exist. Without a constraint, a Gaussian process that is free to take any smooth shape can imitate the straight-line trend: a draw can raise the line and lower the GP by the same amount, or tilt the line one way and the GP the other, and the data cannot tell the two apart. That redundancy is a ridge in the posterior, and it is what made VG09's $q$ hyperparameters sample badly.

The fix removes the redundancy directly. On every posterior draw the unit-amplitude GP is first **least-squares projected out of the directions the mean already spans** — both the constant direction and the linear-in-age direction — with the projection coefficients fitted on the observed rows alone, so that nothing about the reporting grid can move the likelihood. The residual is then **shifted to be exactly zero at the reference age**, pinning its level:

$$\tilde g_U(a) = \eta_U\Big[\big(\tilde u_U(a) - B(a)^{\top}\hat c\big) - \big(\tilde u_U(a_{\text{ref}}) - B(a_{\text{ref}})^{\top}\hat c\big)\Big], \qquad \hat c = \arg\min_c \lVert \tilde u_U - Bc \rVert^2_{\text{observed rows}}$$

with $B = [\,1,\ a_z\,]$ the mean's own basis, and the same construction for $\tilde g_q$. Both parts matter, but they do different work: shifting to zero at the reference age fixes the GP's _level_ against the intercept, while removing the linear direction is what stops the GP trading off against the _slope_. The second is the part that actually resolves VG09's geometry, and a constraint that only pinned a constant would not have.

The reference age is a deliberate model choice — see the glance box above for where it sits relative to the two trend anchors — and it is an identifiability device, not a claim about development. It changes how the model is written, not what shapes it can express.

### Levelling the production ratio off above the high anchor {#sec-clamp}

Above the high age anchor the production ratio's mean is held level rather than being extrapolated along its straight line; the understood mean is not. The reason is asymmetric behaviour past the data: continued upward on the logit scale, the $q$ line runs to near-saturation at the top of the modelled age range, and the flexible term then spends its budget correcting that asymptote instead of describing the ages where the observations are. The understood mean shows the same defect far more mildly and does not saturate, so it is left free.

The corner is rounded rather than sharp, so the mean's transition is smooth and differentiable; the Gaussian process term remains unconstrained there, so the fitted curve itself is not guaranteed monotone. What this means for a reader is confined to the oldest reported ages: at the very top of the reported range the production ratio — and the spoken curve, which is understood multiplied by it — is a levelled-off mean moved only by the Gaussian process, not a trend still being fitted. Below the high anchor the clamp does nothing at all. A registered sensitivity variant that clamps both means as well is fitted and reported under [Robustness](#sec-robustness).

### Why the curves stop at different ages {#sec-caps}

The glance box lists two different reporting caps, and the figures honour them: the words-understood curve and every ratio built from understood — the production ratio, the comprehension-production gap, expected spoken given understood — stop earlier than the words-spoken curve, so the joint-trajectory figures show one line ending before the other.

There are three reasons, and they coincide. Comprehension is recorded on substantially fewer rows than production, and its rows thin out earlier in age, so the evidence runs out sooner. The understood cap is set at 72 months — below the 84-month high trend anchor — because the 72–84 band, while populated, cannot distinguish the Down syndrome child structures, so a comprehension number there depends on which model produced it (see the reporting-ages policy in `docs/models/README.md`). And any quantity that divides spoken by understood inherits the narrower of the two caps by construction. Production has observations well past that point, so it is reported further. The exact ages are in the glance box; they are properties of this fit and are read from it rather than written here.

## Priors

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_priors_table

render_priors_table()
```

The anchors deserve a word about their provenance, because they are not all the same kind of prior. The **low production-ratio anchor** is centred on an independent typically-developing estimate at a comparable age, so it carries outside information. The **high production-ratio anchor and both understood anchors** are frame calibration on this project's own data: they were set so that the prior trend line sits in the region the directly observed comprehension and spoken/understood ratios occupy, because there is no independent norm for Down syndrome comprehension or for the Down syndrome production ratio. That is a legitimate choice, but it is not an external norm and should not be described as one. They are _not_ read off any model's posterior — an earlier generation of $q$ anchors was derived from VG07's posterior fitted to these same data, and [#155](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/pull/155) removed that prior-data double-dipping across the whole Down syndrome joint family. The registered sensitivity variant `u-anchor-broad` reverts the understood anchors to their pre-calibration vague form, and is reported under [Robustness](#sec-robustness).

Stabilisation of the $q$ decomposition comes from the **GP anchor** (@sec-gp-anchor), not from a tight amplitude prior and not from a narrow anchor. The amplitude prior for the production ratio has since been widened from an earlier, tighter setting that was mis-scoped; the table above states what this fit actually used, and the marginal posterior figures in [Diagnostics](#sec-diagnostics) show where the fitted amplitude landed inside it.

Both dispersion blocks use the two-anchor form, with priors stated as $\kappa$ at two reference ages rather than as an intercept and a slope, so each prior is directly comparable with a per-age dispersion estimate and neither shifts meaning if the pool's age distribution changes. These $\kappa$ are _conditional_ quantities: this model carries study and child random intercepts, so $\kappa$ describes what is left once a child's own level is known, not the total spread between children at an age. The prior scales are deliberately wide, because the Down syndrome joint frame is the thinnest the calibration exercise covers and the estimator used there recovers a known $\kappa$ with a one-directional downward bias (the prior medians use the uncorrected calibration — the earlier a-priori bias correction was dropped, as a stated position). What is not in doubt is that the _previous_ prior was wrong in scale: its half-normal slope prior was far too narrow for the fitted concentration trend, leaving the posterior about four standard deviations into its tail with negative contraction. See `docs/models/PRIORS.md`.

## Prior predictive checks

These simulate trajectories from the priors alone, before the data are seen. The figures below are **population mean functions** — study and child effects at zero, no Beta-Binomial counts — so they test the mean structure's priors only and cannot validate the random-effect scales or the dispersion priors. Read them as a plausibility test with four criteria: young children should usually sit near the floor on both outcomes; older trajectories should not be forced towards the ceiling; the simulated comprehension-production gap should be able to open and to close again; and the simulated production ratio should be able to reach both low and high values across the age range. A prior that failed any of these would be shaping the answer rather than permitting it. The falsifier to watch for is the opposite of the usual one: if the prior spoken curves were _too narrow_, the stabilising priors would be doing substantive work that belongs to the data.

The figures below satisfy those criteria — the prior envelopes are wide at every age, and neither outcome is pinned to a floor or a ceiling anywhere in the range.

![Population mean-function trajectories for words understood, drawn from the priors alone.](prior_samples_u.png){#fig-prior-samples-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Population mean-function trajectories for words spoken, drawn from the priors alone.](prior_samples_s.png){#fig-prior-samples-s .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Population mean-function trajectories for the production ratio $q(a)$, drawn from the priors alone.](prior_samples_q.png){#fig-prior-samples-q .lightbox fig-align="left"}

::: {.callout-important title="Is the VG09 geometry resolved? Yes."}

This is the question VG10 exists to answer, so it is answered here rather than left to the reader.

VG09's failure was concentrated in the production-ratio block: its $q$ anchors, the $q$ GP hyperparameters, and the two $q$ random-effect scales showed marginal R-hat and tail-ESS problems, the signature of the trend/GP ridge described in @sec-gp-anchor. Under VG10's anchored geometry every one of those parameters clears both hard thresholds comfortably in the diagnostics table above — check the rows for `p_slope_low_q`, `p_slope_hi_q`, `eta_q`, `ell_q`, `ell_unit_q`, `tau_q` and `tau_subj_q`, and the pair plot for the ridges that produced the problem. The reported R-hat maximum and ESS minimum across the whole parameter set are in `diagnostics_summary.json` and are summarised by the gate; both pass.

That is the whole of the claim. The anchor fixed a _sampling_ pathology, and a resolved geometry is a precondition for believing the numbers below — not itself a finding about vocabulary. Any soft-tier caveat this fit carries is disclosed in the block at the top of this section and applies on top of this verdict.

:::

## Findings

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_headline_quantities

render_headline_quantities()
```

Four things in that table carry the substance of the model.

**Comprehension leads production, and the lead is measurable in both time and words.** The fastest growth in words understood arrives well before the fastest growth in words spoken, and the gap between what the reference (zero-effect) child understands and what they say opens, peaks, and then closes again over the reported range. That rise-and-fall shape is the model's central descriptive result: expressive vocabulary is not simply a smaller copy of receptive vocabulary, it is a delayed one.

**The production ratio is the mechanism.** $q$ rises across the whole reported range — the fraction of understood words that a child also says grows with age — and the table gives the age at which it reaches one half. That single crossing is the most quotable number the model produces, and it is read off the median curve rather than being the posterior median of the crossing itself.

**Dispersion increases with age on both outcomes.** The variance-inflation readings in the last two rows grow, meaning that by school age an observation carries a small fraction of the information a Binomial count of the same size would. This is the quantitative reason the predictive bands widen so much at the top of the range, and it vindicates the prior change described under [Priors](#priors): the legacy slope prior was far too narrow for a concentration trend this steep, and the two-anchor form lets the dataset both its direction and its size.

**Children differ more than studies do, and they differ most in conversion.**

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_variation_table

render_variation_table()
```

Both child scales exceed both study scales, so the pooled cohort is not simply an artefact of mixing studies with different recruitment. And the child scale on the production ratio exceeds the child scale on comprehension: children of the same age differ _more_ in how much of their comprehension they speak than in how much they comprehend. Expressive conversion is the more individually variable trait, which is a substantive claim about Down syndrome vocabulary development and not a modelling artefact.

The practical consequence runs through every table below. Wherever a population-level and a subject-marginal interval are printed side by side, the second is several times the width of the first, and it is the second that answers a question about an individual child.

### Joint trajectory

### Production ratio

The production ratio $q(a) = p_S(a) / p_U(a)$ is the fraction of understood words expected also to be spoken at age $a$ — equivalently, the expected number of words spoken per word understood. A value of one half means that half of the words a child understands are words they also say.

![The population-level production ratio against age, with uncertainty intervals. It rises across the reported range: older children say a larger share of what they understand.](production_rate.png){#fig-production-rate .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The same population-level ratio plotted against expected words understood instead of against age. Read it as: children at this level of comprehension convert this fraction of it — the evidence for the claim that conversion improves as comprehension grows.](production_rate_by_understood.png){#fig-production-rate-by-understood .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The ratio of **posterior predictive spoken and understood counts**, which is a different quantity from $q(a)$ above and should be read separately. It is a ratio of two noisy counts for individual children rather than a ratio of two means, so it is both noisier and, at young ages where the denominator is small, biased in ways $q(a)$ is not.](production_rate_predictive.png){#fig-production-rate-predictive .lightbox fig-align="left"}

### Comprehension-production gap

![The expected difference in word counts between understanding and production, against age. It rises to a peak and then closes.](comprehension_production_gap.png){#fig-gap .lightbox fig-align="left"}

Conclude from this figure that the gap is a phase rather than a permanent state: it widens through the preschool years, peaks, and then narrows as the production ratio climbs. The peak's size and the age it occurs at are in the [Findings](#findings) table, computed from the same CSV this figure is drawn from. The narrowing does not mean the two vocabularies converge within the reported range — they do not — only that production is catching up.

### Words understood versus words spoken

![Expected words understood against expected words spoken, as **population-level** curves. Each line is one posterior draw; age runs along each curve rather than being an axis.](understood_vs_spoken.png){#fig-understood-vs-spoken .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The same pairing as **subject-marginal predictive counts**. The spread between the curves here includes between-child variation, which the population-level figure above excludes.](understood_vs_spoken_predictive.png){#fig-understood-vs-spoken-predictive .lightbox fig-align="left"}

Conclude from the pair that the relationship between the two vocabularies is not a fixed proportion: the curves bend upward, so each additional understood word is converted to speech at a higher rate later than earlier.

### Receptive to expressive (cross-sectional)

**How are receptive and expressive vocabulary related cross-sectionally?** The joint model links the two structurally through the production ratio $q(a) = P(\text{speak} \mid \text{understood})$: the expected number of words a child _says_ is the number they _understand_ scaled by $q(a)$,

$$\mathbb{E}[\,\text{spoken} \mid \text{understood} = N,\ \text{age} = a\,] \approx N \cdot q(a).$$

Thus $q(a)$ is an age-dependent cross-sectional conversion proportion — the expected number of words spoken per word understood under the model — **not** evidence that increasing a particular child's receptive vocabulary causes a corresponding expressive gain. Most of these data are cross-sectional, and the comparison is between different children of different ages, not within one child over time.

The figure below reads the fitted association directly, and is the most practitioner-facing thing this model produces: for children with Down syndrome at several ages, it maps words understood on the x axis to expected words spoken on the y axis, with the shaded band the 89% interval on $q(a)$ and the dashed line the ceiling that no child can exceed. Each fan line is straight because its slope is a single number — the **population** production ratio at that age. It is therefore an expectation for the zero-effect reference child in the average study at that age and comprehension level, not a prediction for a named child, whose own conversion rate carries the child random effect reported in the [Findings](#findings) variation table. The per-age posterior of $q(a)$ is tabulated under [Production ratio](#production-ratio) above.

![Predicted words spoken given words understood, at several ages. The fan opens with age: the same comprehension converts to more speech in an older child.](spoken_given_understood.png){#fig-spoken-given-understood .lightbox fig-align="left"}

## Posterior predictions -- words understood

### Summary at selected ages

$p$ is the latent success probability — the underlying proportion of the reference inventory a child is expected to understand at a given age. $Ey$ is the expected count implied by $p$. $Y$ is a draw from the posterior predictive distribution. Read the `*_population_*` columns for the zero-effect reference child in the average study (approximately the median child, not the mean of children), and the `*_subject_marginal_*` and `Y_*` columns for where a single unseen child might fall; the latter are much the wider, and are the ones to quote about an individual.

posterior_summary_u

### Median trend

![Median predicted words understood with uncertainty intervals, against the observed data.](posterior_predictive_median_trend_u.png){#fig-trend-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The same trend, smoothed for presentation. The underlying numbers are unchanged.](posterior_predictive_median_trend_u_smoothed.png){#fig-trend-u-smooth .lightbox fig-align="left"}

Conclude that the fitted trend tracks the observations across the range where they are dense, and that the observed points scatter widely around it — the scatter, not the line, is what a single child's outcome resembles.

### Cross-sectional age derivative

![Rate of change of expected words understood with age, in words gained per month.](expected_learning_rate_u.png){#fig-rate-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The same derivative, smoothed for presentation.](expected_learning_rate_u_smoothed.png){#fig-rate-u-smooth .lightbox fig-align="left"}

This is the slope of the fitted age trajectory: it describes how expected vocabulary differs between children of different ages. It is **not** a within-child learning rate. Conclude that comprehension growth is fastest in the early part of the range and slows thereafter — the peak rate and its age are in the [Findings](#findings) table — and that where the interval spans zero at the top of the range, the model cannot distinguish continued growth from a plateau. The unsmoothed curve carries wiggles from the Gaussian process that the smoothed version damps; do not read a small local dip in the raw curve as a developmental stage.

### Dispersion $\kappa$ -- understood

![How the understood dispersion parameter changes with age, with uncertainty intervals.](posterior_kappa_u.png){#fig-kappa-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

Lower $\kappa$ means **greater** between-child variability relative to the mean; higher $\kappa$ means less. The direction is easy to misread, so read this figure as _falling $\kappa$ = children becoming more spread out_, and read the [Findings](#findings) table, which restates the same thing as a variance inflation factor where a larger number means a wider spread. Conclude that residual spread grows with age even after each child's own level is accounted for.

## Robustness {#sec-robustness}

A conclusion that depends on one arbitrary modelling choice is not a conclusion. Registered sensitivity variants refit this model with a single deliberate change and compare the reported quantities against the model of record's own 89% intervals; the harness records a verdict per variant and declines to give one where the comparison is not sound.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

from IPython.display import Markdown, display


def comparison_path(name):
    """Locate a comparison artefact from wherever this report is rendered."""
    for base in (Path("../../comparisons"), Path("comparisons"), Path("../comparisons")):
        candidate = base / name
        if candidate.is_file():
            return candidate
    return None


robustness_path = comparison_path("sensitivity/robustness_matrix_vg10.csv")
if robustness_path is None:
    display(Markdown(
        "_The sensitivity comparison has not been computed into this output root, "
        "so no robustness matrix is available for this render._"
    ))
else:
    robustness = pd.read_csv(robustness_path)
    display(robustness[[
        "variant",
        "status",
        "n_within_ci",
        "n_checked",
        "max_abs_delta",
        "quantities_outside_ci",
        "verdict",
        "variant_fit_utc",
    ]])
```

The table lists every registered VG10 sensitivity variant, read from the comparison harness's own output. `n_within_ci` of `n_checked` is how many reported quantities fell inside the model of record's 89% interval; `max_abs_delta` is the largest movement, in the units of the quantity concerned. Rows whose `status` records no fit have not been run.

Read the `verdict` column rather than the deltas. Variants marked robust moved nothing outside the baseline's own intervals, so the reported conclusions do not depend on that choice. A variant marked **sensitive** did move quantities outside, and is a live caveat on everything above it in this report: where the harness names a quantity in `quantities_outside_ci`, statements about that quantity at the ages where the two fits disagree should be read as conditional on the modelling choice the variant changes. Two comparisons carry no verdict at all — one because it was fitted against a baseline that has since changed and needs refitting, the other because too few of its reported ages are shared with the baseline for a comparison to mean anything. Both are disclosed rather than quietly dropped, and neither should be read as evidence either way.

Three of the registered variants -- `paired-only`, `fallback-dispersion` and `marginal-moments` -- vary one thing this report has previously only disclosed: the treatment of spoken rows with no usable understood count. 455 of the 1,428 spoken observations take that branch (444 have no comprehension total, 11 record more spoken than understood words), and the substitute likelihood $S\sim\mathrm{BetaBinomial}(N,p_Uq,\kappa_S)$ has the paired model's mean but not its variance. The discrepancy is exact and signed: the true marginal is more dispersed than the substitute exactly when $q\kappa_S > \kappa_U$, and less when the inequality reverses, so which way this model errs is a question about its own fitted concentrations rather than a structural bias in a known direction. `paired-only` drops those rows and bounds the effect; `fallback-dispersion` keeps them and measures it with one signed scalar that nests the default at zero; `marginal-moments` removes it by matching the true marginal's first two moments. Read them together: the first two disagreeing would mean the branch matters and the rows carry something the paired rows do not, and `marginal-moments` moving nothing would mean the approximation was harmless here after all. The branch-stratified rows of the predictive-calibration table are the companion diagnostic: the two branches differ systematically in age and study composition, so a well-behaved pooled row can hide a badly-behaved branch.


### Parameter recovery

Parameter recovery simulates a dataset from the model at a known parameter draw, refits the model to it through the same pipeline, and asks whether the posterior covers the truth it was generated from.

```{python}
recovery_path = comparison_path("recovery/recovery_matrix_vg10.csv")
if recovery_path is None:
    display(Markdown(
        "_No parameter-recovery comparison is available in this output root._"
    ))
else:
    recovery = pd.read_csv(recovery_path)
    display(recovery[[
        "replicate",
        "truth_source",
        "converged",
        "n_targets",
        "n_within_ci89",
        "coverage_ci89",
        "coverage_ci50",
        "max_abs_z",
        "verdict",
    ]])
```

The rows are the individual replicates and a pooled summary, read from the comparison harness's own output.

Three caveats, all of which limit what this table can support.

**Coverage is below nominal, and it is not specific to this model.** Across three replicates VG10 covers 0.72 of its targets at the 89% level and 0.31 at the 50%, and two of the three replicates were not assessable because their own fits did not converge. The correlated successor VG20 was run at the same tier and replicate count and does better on every one of those figures (0.78 and 0.41), so this is a property of the engine and the `test` sampling tier rather than of either model's structure. It is a real limitation on what this table can certify, and it is the same limitation for both.

**`tau_subj_u` comes back below its truth in every replicate** — z = −1.39, −2.28, −0.87 here, and −1.94, −1.24, −1.58 on VG20: six of six across the two models, none of which carries `subject_variance_partition`. That matters beyond this page, because the same downward bias in the between-child scale was found on VG12, which *does* carry the partition, and attributed to it ([#225](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/225)). Six replicates on two unpartitioned models say the partition cannot be the whole cause. Six replicates cannot say what is.

**An earlier version of this section reported the `a1-tau-age-varying` variant instead**, on the stated grounds that no recovery had been run on VG10 as registered. One had, from 2026-08-16; the page went on disclaiming a near-neighbour for three days while the model's own matrix sat unread beside it. Corrected 2026-08-19.

**Not every replicate is assessable.** A replicate is scored only if its own fit's convergence is confirmed; the `converged` column shows which were, and the pooled row names how many of the replicates it covers. A non-converged replicate is excluded rather than counted as a failure.

**A handful of replicates is indicative only.** The harness says so in its own verdict, and the wording is worth taking literally: this is coverage measured over correlated quantities from a small number of draws, not simulation-based calibration. It can reveal a gross problem; it cannot certify that the posterior is calibrated. The quantities that fall outside their intervals most often are named in the full per-replicate files alongside this matrix, and they cluster on the production-ratio block and the random-effect scales — the parameters this model family finds hardest, which is the expected place for recovery to be weakest.

## Limits

- **Age is not a mechanism.** Everything reported here is an association with age, not an effect of it, and the production ratio is a conversion proportion rather than a causal pathway from comprehension to speech.
- **The reference inventory is a harmonisation.** Counts from different checklists are placed on a common scale; it is a unit of measurement, not an instrument any child sat. The registered `dse-native-only` variant probes that assumption, and the [Robustness](#sec-robustness) table reports what it found.
- **Beyond the high anchor the production ratio does not extrapolate — it is held level** (@sec-clamp). Quantities quoted at the very top of the reported range are a levelled-off mean moved by the flexible term alone.
- **Repeated measurement is modelled as a per-child offset only.** Children are not given their own slopes: every child's latent trajectory is parallel, relative standing is fixed at every age, and rank changes are impossible by construction — stability of developmental tracking is an assumption here, not an estimate. VG16 adds a within-child cross-lag and VG19 a child slope; this model has neither.
- **For spoken-only children, mainly the product of the two child effects is identified.** Children contributing spoken observations but no understood observation at any wave — over 150 children in the current frame — chiefly inform the product of their comprehension and production-ratio effects, so the individual split for them is driven by the hierarchy and the priors. This compounds the superseded independence assumption disclosed at the top of this report.
- **Where the data thin out, the curve is the model.** The `n_obs` column in the monthly tables shows where that begins, and it begins well before the top of both reported ranges.
- **The Down syndrome pool masks several documented defect classes by default.** Reinstating the masked implausible-production rows is a registered variant; see [Robustness](#sec-robustness) for its current status.
